name: Telugu
region: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, with large communities across India and abroad
about: Telugu is one of India's classical languages, and because almost every word ends in a vowel, it was nicknamed the Italian of the East. It is also one of the fastest growing languages among Indian communities in the United States.
pronunciation: Almost every Telugu word ends in a vowel, so let words flow smoothly into each other.
Long vowels matter, so stretch the aa in namaskaaram and the ee in meeru.
Retroflex sounds like the d in rendu are made with the tongue curled back, just as in Hindi.
Stress is light and even, so avoid punching one syllable hard the way English does.

lessons.intro: Namaskaaram! Let's begin Telugu with the warm, everyday greetings you'll hear all over Hyderabad and Andhra.
lessons.tip: Telugu has a respectful you, meeru, and a casual you, nuvvu. Use meeru with elders, strangers and anyone you've just met.

phrases.note: Namaskaaram is the respectful hello, usually said with folded hands. Friends often just say hi or ela unnaav.
Meeru elaa unnaaru is the polite way to ask how someone is. With close friends you can say ela unnaav, or simply baagunnaaraa, meaning are you well.
Nenu baagunnaanu means I am fine. People often reply with just baagunnaanu, and then ask back, meeru, meaning and you.
Dhanyavaadaalu is the proper thank you. In daily life many Telugu speakers simply say thanks in English, which is perfectly natural.
Kshaminchandi means please forgive me. It works both as sorry and as excuse me when you need someone's attention.
Vellostaanu literally means I'll go and come back. Telugu speakers avoid saying just I'm going, because it sounds final, so this is the polite goodbye.

lessons.intro: Now let's introduce ourselves in Telugu. People love chatting about names and home towns, so these phrases will open many doors.
lessons.tip: Telugu verbs come at the end of the sentence, and the word for is often disappears. Naa peru Priya is literally my name Priya.

phrases.note: Naa peru Priya means my name is Priya. Just swap in your own name at the end.
Mee peru emiti is the polite way to ask someone's name. In casual speech you'll also hear mee peru enti.
Meedi e ooru literally means which town is yours. It's the most natural way to ask where someone is from.
This means I have come from India. Bhaaratadesham is India. In everyday speech you can also say naadi India.
This means meeting you makes me happy. It's polite and warm, perfect for a first meeting.
Naaku konchem telugu vachchu literally means a little Telugu comes to me. People will be delighted to hear you try.

lessons.intro: Time for numbers! Telugu counting is easy and musical. Let's count together and learn today, tomorrow and yesterday.
lessons.tip: In cities like Hyderabad people mix English numbers into Telugu, especially for prices and times, so don't be surprised to hear time entha, ten thirty.

phrases.note: Okati, rendu, moodu, naalugu, aidu are one to five. Notice how each number ends in a soft vowel.
Aaru, edu, enimidi, tommidi, padi are six to ten. Keep the aa in aaru long and clear.
Time entha ayindi literally means how much time has it become. This is how everyone asks the time. The formal word for time is samayam.
Eeroju means today, literally this day. You'll also hear ivvaala in some regions.
Repu means tomorrow. Repu kaluddaam means let's meet tomorrow.
Ninna means yesterday. Say it with a clear double n sound in the middle.

lessons.intro: Andhra food is famous for its spice! Let's learn how to order, ask prices and pay like a local.
lessons.tip: Adding andi to the end of a sentence makes it more respectful. Shopkeepers will appreciate a polite idi entha andi.

phrases.note: Idi entha means how much is this. Add andi at the end, idi entha andi, to sound extra polite.
Dhara chaalaa ekkuva means the price is too high. It's a gentle way to start bargaining at a market.
This means please give me some drinking water. Manchineellu literally means good water, the word for drinking water.
Nenu shaakaahaarini means I am vegetarian. In restaurants it's just as common to say nenu non veg tinanu, meaning I don't eat non veg.
This means it is very tasty. A simple chaalaa baagundi, very nice, will also make the cook smile.
Billu teesukurandi means please bring the bill. The ending andi makes the request polite.

lessons.intro: Let's get around! These phrases will help you find your way through busy Telugu streets and stations.
lessons.tip: Telugu speakers often mix English words like station, bus and left into sentences. Using them is perfectly natural and widely understood.

phrases.note: Railway station ekkada undi means where is the railway station. Ekkada means where, and undi means it is.
Edama vaipu tiragandi means turn towards the left. Edama is left.
Kudi vaipu tiragandi means turn towards the right. Kudi is right.
Nerugaa vellandi means go straight. You'll often hear the mixed form straight gaa vellandi too.
Entha dooram undi means how far is it. Dooram means distance.
This is the polite please help me. In casual speech people say konchem help cheyyandi.

lessons.intro: Our last Telugu lesson! These everyday phrases will keep any conversation going, even when you get a little lost.
lessons.tip: Telugu has different words for no. Kaadu means it is not, ledu means there isn't, and vaddu means I don't want it.

phrases.note: Avunu means yes and kaadu means no, as in that's not so. You'll also hear a casual haa for yes.
Naaku artham kaaledu means I didn't understand. Telugu uses the past tense here, as in the meaning didn't reach me.
This means please speak slowly. Nemmadigaa means slowly or gently.
Deeni artham emiti means what is the meaning of this. Point at a word or sign and ask.
Naaku idi nachchindi literally means this pleased me. It's how you say I like it.
Shubha raatri means good night. In everyday life many people simply say good night in English.
